title: Knowledge Check 6 - Lessons 26-30
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 26-30 - OmniScripts. Pass with 80% or higher to move toward unlocking the cert prep exam.

questions.question: An OmniScript fetches an account, but the journey only displays the account name and status. What is the better fetch design?
options: Fetch the entire account object and store it in the data JSON
Fetch only the name and status fields the journey needs, and store them under a stable name
Fetch nothing and let the user type the data
Fetch the account in every Step
questions.explanation: Fetch should be lazy and targeted: pull only what the journey needs. Fetching the whole object wastes a round trip, fetching nothing loses real data, and re-fetching in every Step is redundant. Store the needed fields under a stable name for later reference.

questions.question: A consultant adds a new branch to an OmniScript that captures a 'preferred contact time' field. The save uses a Data Mapper. What must the consultant do?
options: Nothing, the Data Mapper handles all fields automatically
Update the Data Mapper's save mapping to include the new field
Add a new Integration Procedure
Remove the branch
questions.explanation: The save mapping must include every field captured on every branch, or the new field is silently dropped. A Data Mapper does not automatically pick up new fields, and adding an IP or removing the branch does not address the missing mapping.

questions.question: A fetch stage in an OmniScript can fail when the external service is down. What is the correct design for this failure?
options: Let it fail silently and continue
Read the returned status and route the failure to a user-facing message or a log
Retry forever until it succeeds
Skip the fetch and use empty data
questions.explanation: Error handling belongs in the flow: the fetch should return a status the OmniScript reads, and failures should surface to the user or a log. Failing silently hides the problem, retrying forever blocks the user, and using empty data produces wrong results.

questions.question: An OmniScript must collect a list of line items, each with a product, quantity, and price. What is the correct element structure?
options: A single Step with one text Input for the whole list
A repeatable Block containing product, quantity, and price Inputs
Three separate Steps, one per field
A read-only Input
questions.explanation: A list of line items is a repeating group, so a repeatable Block is the right structure: each instance holds product, quantity, and price, and writes to its own data JSON node. A single text input cannot hold structured line items, separate Steps fragment the task, and a read-only input cannot capture data.

questions.question: A consultant needs to show a fetched account name to the user for confirmation, but the user should not edit it. What element should be used?
options: An editable text Input
A read-only Input that displays the value from the data JSON
A repeatable Block
A picklist
questions.explanation: A read-only Input displays a value from the data JSON without allowing edits, which is exactly the confirmation use case. An editable input invites changes, a repeatable Block is for lists, and a picklist is for a fixed set of choices.

questions.question: Two Inputs in an OmniScript are accidentally given the same data JSON name. What is the result?
options: The OmniScript fails to deploy
The two Inputs collide and one overwrites the other in the data JSON
Both values are stored in an array
The second Input is ignored silently
questions.explanation: The data JSON name is the contract, and two Inputs with the same name collide, with one overwriting the other. This corrupts the data the downstream logic reads. Names must be unique and deliberate.

questions.question: An OmniScript must show a running total of line items to the user as they add them. Where should the total be computed?
options: In a Formula element that reads the line items from the data JSON
In the Data Mapper that saves the record
In a read-only Input
In a validation rule
questions.explanation: The total is needed for display inside the OmniScript, so a Formula that reads the line items and writes the result to the data JSON is correct. A Data Mapper computes for the saved record, a read-only input displays a stored value, and a validation rule checks input.

questions.question: A value is needed both for display in the OmniScript and in the saved record. What is the correct approach?
options: Compute it in both a Formula and a Data Mapper
Compute it once, in the place that owns the value, and reference it from the other
Compute it in a Display Function only
Hardcode the value
questions.explanation: Computing the same value in two places is a maintenance hazard because the two can drift. Compute it once in the owner location and reference it from the other. A Display Function only renders, and hardcoding is not a real solution.

questions.question: A Formula references a field that is only populated on one branch of the OmniScript. On the other branch the field is empty. What is the risk?
options: The formula always works
The formula breaks or returns an unexpected value on the branch where the field is empty
The OmniScript fails to deploy
The field is auto-populated
questions.explanation: A formula that assumes a field is always present breaks when the field is empty, which happens on branches that skip it. The formula must handle empty and missing inputs explicitly, and it should be tested against the empty case.

questions.question: An OmniScript needs a custom map picker that standard elements cannot provide. What is the appropriate approach?
options: Use a standard picklist instead
Add an LWC Embed that renders the custom map picker and writes the selection to the data JSON
Add a text Input for the location
Use a FlexCard
questions.explanation: When a standard element cannot express the interaction, an LWC Embed is the right tool: it renders the custom component and writes the result to the data JSON. A standard picklist or text input cannot provide a map picker, and a FlexCard is a display component, not an input.

questions.question: A consultant is deciding whether to build a custom LWC or use a standard element for a simple picklist. What is the better choice?
options: Build the custom LWC for more control
Use the standard picklist, since it already solves the interaction with less cost
Use a FlexCard
Use a Formula
questions.explanation: Standard components should be the default because they cover most needs with less build, test, and maintenance cost. A custom LWC is warranted only when a standard element cannot do the job. A FlexCard is display, and a Formula computes a value.

questions.question: An LWC Embed in an OmniScript writes its result to the data JSON under a name that does not match what the save logic expects. What is the result?
options: The save logic reads the correct value automatically
The value is stored but the save logic reads a different or empty value, so the data is lost or wrong
The OmniScript fails to deploy
The LWC is ignored
questions.explanation: The data JSON name is the contract. If the LWC writes under a name the save logic does not expect, the save reads a different or empty value and the data is lost or wrong. The contract must be agreed and matched before building.

questions.question: An address capture sub-journey is used in three different parent OmniScripts. What is the appropriate design?
options: Duplicate the address Steps in each parent
Build the address capture once as a child OmniScript and invoke it from each parent
Use a FlexCard for the address
Use a Formula
questions.explanation: When the same sub-journey is reused by multiple parents, build it once as a child OmniScript and invoke it from each, which reduces duplication and keeps behavior consistent. Duplicating the Steps in each parent is the maintenance burden the child avoids, and a FlexCard or Formula does not capture the address.

questions.question: An OmniScript must show the user a branded summary of their order before they confirm. The user does not edit anything on this screen. What is the appropriate component?
options: A child OmniScript
A FlexCard that renders the order summary in a branded layout
An LWC Embed
A repeatable Block
questions.explanation: The user only needs to see the order summary, so a FlexCard that renders the data in a branded layout is correct. A child OmniScript is for interactive sub-journeys that capture data, an LWC is for custom interactions, and a repeatable Block is for collecting lists.

questions.question: A consultant is deciding between a child OmniScript and a FlexCard for a step where the user must enter payment details. What is the correct choice?
options: A FlexCard, because it displays data clearly
A child OmniScript, because the user must interact and capture data
A Formula
A read-only Input
questions.explanation: Entering payment details is an interaction that captures data, so a child OmniScript (or the parent's own Steps) is correct. A FlexCard only displays data and cannot capture the payment. A Formula computes a value, and a read-only input cannot accept the entry.
